subject.title: Digital Logic
subject.description: Number systems and codes, Boolean algebra and gates, minimisation, combinational and sequential circuits, computer arithmetic and IEEE-754 floating point, built from first principles with animated circuits and every GATE question mapped.

chapters.title: Number systems, codes and floating point
chapters.summary: Place value in any base, the binary family, fractions and fixed point, signed numbers and complements, floating point and IEEE-754 (formats, special values, arithmetic and rounding), and the codes digital systems use.

chapters.title: Boolean algebra and logic gates
chapters.summary: Gates and truth tables, the laws of Boolean algebra (duality, De Morgan, consensus, Shannon), XOR/XNOR algebra and custom operators, minterms, maxterms and counting functions, universal gates and functional completeness, and how to analyse gate circuits and their timing.

chapters.title: Minimisation
chapters.summary: Karnaugh maps from two to six variables, prime and essential prime implicants, don't-cares, minimal SOP and POS, the Quine–McCluskey tabular method with PI charts and Petrick's method, variable-entered maps, and how minimal forms become NAND/NOR circuits: literal and gate counts, static hazards and shared terms.

chapters.title: Arithmetic circuits
chapters.summary: Half and full adders and subtractors designed from their truth tables, ripple-carry adders and their delay models, carry look-ahead with generate and propagate, multi-level and hybrid adders, the adder–subtractor with overflow and status flags, the BCD adder circuit, array multipliers and their delay, and sequential and Booth multiplier hardware.

chapters.title: Combinational building blocks
chapters.summary: Designing combinational circuits from a specification, code converters, multiplexers and function realisation with implementation tables and MUX trees, decoders, demultiplexers, encoders and priority encoders, magnitude comparators and parity circuits, ROM, PLA and PAL sizing, and stuck-at faults with test inputs.

The idea: a digit counts bundles

attrs.title: Digits count bundles, positions name the bundle size

c:
Think of a shop that only uses bundles of three: loose items, packets of 3, boxes of 3 packets
(9 items), crates of 3 boxes (27 items). To record 46 items you fill crates first: one crate
(27), then two boxes (18), no packets, and one loose item. The record reads

Each position holds the number of bundles of one size, and the sizes grow by the same factor
(here 3) as you move left. A position can never hold 3 or more, because three of anything
would be packed into one bundle of the next size. That one rule, "pack as soon as you reach
the base", is all of positional notation. Our everyday decimal is the same shop with bundles
of ten.

An odometer is the same shop in motion. Watch a counter whose wheels only know the digits 0, 1
and 2: when a wheel would reach 3 it rolls back to 0 and nudges its neighbour forward.
Notice what the counter shows after three counts:

three and nothing loose, which is three. That is why "10" means

in every base:

blocks.title: Binary, octal and hex on one card

c:
Binary is the language of the hardware, but long strings of bits are hard for people to read.
Octal and hexadecimal fix that, and they fix it

: because 8 and 16 are powers of 2,
you convert by cutting the bit string into groups, with no division at all. In this lesson you
learn why grouping works, how to do it without the classic off-by-a-group slip, how to move
between octal, hex and base 4 through binary, how to read a "powers of 16" sum straight off as
hex, and how to add, subtract and multiply directly in base 8 or 16.

gave the general tools: expand to read, divide to write. They
work for every base, but for bases 2, 4, 8 and 16 they are the slow road. Everything in later
chapters is written in these bases: memory addresses and instruction fields in hex, Unix
permissions in octal, K-map cells and register contents in binary. The 2's-complement patterns
of
are also usually given in hex.

c:
In base 2 the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, … Look at them three at a time from the
right: (1, 2, 4), then (8, 16, 32) which is 8 × (1, 2, 4), then (64, 128, 256), which is
64 × (1, 2, 4). Each block of three places is the first block scaled by a power of 8.
So a block of three bits is a number from 0 to 7 counting units of

units of

paying with ₹10 notes bundled in hundreds: a bundle is an exact multiple of a note, so you can
count bundles without unpacking them. Blocks of four places scale by 16 the same way, which
gives hexadecimal.

The idea: cutting a cake in halves

You may cut a cake only in half, then cut pieces in half again, and so on. You can serve exactly
a half, a quarter, three-eighths, five-sixteenths: any sum of these binary pieces. But you can
never serve

one fifth of the cake, however many times you cut: you can only get
closer and closer (a quarter is too much, three-sixteenths too little, …).
That is binary fractions in a nutshell. The pieces available are

, and a value is exactly representable only if it is a finite sum of them. A base-10
"cake" can be cut into tenths, so it serves one fifth (0.2) easily, but it cannot serve one
third. Which fractions come out exactly depends on the base.

attrs.title: Further depth: where the formats came from

c:
Before 1985 every manufacturer had its own floating point: IBM used base 16 with an excess-64
exponent (the GATE 2002 format is essentially IBM's single precision), DEC used a hidden bit with
a different bias, and Cray had no gradual underflow. Programs gave different answers on different
machines. IEEE-754 (1985, revised 2008 and 2019) fixed base 2, the hidden bit, the biases, the
special values and the rounding rules, which is why the next lesson can be so precise.

attrs.term: Why ties go to the even neighbour

c:
A tie happens when the exact value is exactly halfway between two floats. Always rounding ties up
would push long sums upward on average (every tie adds half an ulp). Choosing the neighbour with an
even last bit rounds up about half the time and down the other half, so the errors cancel on
average. It also makes the result deterministic: there is exactly one even neighbour.

c:
is a dictionary: it says which bit string stands for which symbol. Plain binary is one
such dictionary, and a very good one for arithmetic, but it is not the best for everything.
In this lesson you meet the codes digital systems actually use for decimal digits (BCD,
excess-3, 2421), for positions and counters (Gray code), and for catching and fixing errors
(parity and Hamming codes). You will learn how to convert into and out of each, how to tell
whether a code is weighted or self-complementing, why a Gray code never glitches, and how three
parity bits can locate any single flipped bit in a 7-bit word.
It uses only place value and grouping from Lessons

(5–7). The next lesson,

of K-maps (Chapter 3), code converters (BCD → excess-3, binary → Gray) are classic combinational
design problems (Chapter 5), BCD and excess-3 addition are in

c:
A calculator shows decimal digits, so it is convenient to store each digit in its own 4-bit
box, even though that wastes 6 of the 16 patterns. A rotary knob must never report a wildly
wrong position while it is between two positions, so consecutive positions should differ in a
single bit. A memory chip wants to notice, and ideally fix, a bit flipped by noise, so it adds
a few check bits. Each need picks a different dictionary. None of them changes the numbers; they
change only how numbers are spelled in bits.

attrs.title: Pay only at the edges of each run

c:
Plain shift-and-add pays once for every 1 in the multiplier, so a multiplier full of 1s is
expensive. Booth pays only where the bits

: once where a run of 1s begins (a subtraction)
and once where it ends (an addition). Inside a run, and inside a run of 0s, it only shifts. So the
cost of a multiplier is the number of its run boundaries, which can be far fewer than its 1s
(long runs) or far more (alternating bits).

Reading a circuit, gate by gate

A recipe says: whisk the eggs, melt the butter, then fold the melted butter into the whisked eggs.
Each step uses ingredients or the results of earlier steps, and you cannot fold before both earlier
steps are done. A circuit is the same: each gate uses circuit inputs or the outputs of gates further
left, and a gate's output is known only once all of its inputs are. So you read a circuit by naming
each intermediate result and working from left to right, exactly as you would follow the recipe.

A circuit is a set of gates whose outputs feed other gates. To find what it computes, give every
gate output a name, then either follow one input row through the circuit or write each gate's
expression and substitute.

Negative logic reads every gate as its dual: AND ↔ OR, NAND ↔ NOR, XOR ↔ XNOR.

In CMOS, the most common logic family, a NAND gate is two transistors in series to ground and two in
parallel to the supply; a NOR is the other way round. Series transistors are slower, and the
pull-up (PMOS) transistors are the slower kind, so a NOR's series PMOS pair makes it slower and
larger than a NAND. That is why NAND, not NOR, is the workhorse universal gate in practice (Lesson 5),
and why an inverting gate is cheaper than a non-inverting one: an AND gate is physically a NAND
followed by an inverter.

usually smaller, circuit that computes the same thing. This lesson turns the rules into an algebra.
You will see the handful of postulates everything rests on, prove the famous laws from them
(absorption, De Morgan, consensus), learn the duality principle that gives you every law twice for
the price of once, split any function in two with Shannon's expansion, and solve systems of Boolean
equations. Twelve GATE questions test exactly these skills.

The postulates and the duality principle

attrs.title: Every rule has a mirror image

c:
Look at the switch pictures again. "Switches in parallel with one stuck closed: the lamp is on" and
"switches in series with one stuck open: the lamp is off" are the same fact seen in a mirror that
swaps series with parallel and closed with open. Boolean algebra has that mirror built in: swap AND
with OR and 0 with 1 in any true law and you get another true law. Half of every list of laws is
therefore free, and when you forget a law you can often recover it from its twin.

An algebra is a set of values with operations and a short list of axioms (postulates) from which
everything else is proved. For Boolean algebra the standard list is due to Huntington.

attrs.name: Duality principle

c: If an identity can be proved from the postulates, its dual is also an identity.
a proof is a chain of steps, each justified by a postulate; dualise every step.

Each of the six postulates is either self-dual (closure, non-triviality) or comes paired with its
dual (identities, commutativity, distributivity, complements). Take any proof of an identity and
replace every expression in it by its dual. Each step that used a postulate now uses that
postulate's dual, which is also a postulate, so every step is still valid. The last line of the new
chain is the dual identity. Hence one proof gives two theorems.

De Morgan's laws and complementing expressions

attrs.title: Not (rain or snow) means no rain and no snow

c:
"It is not true that it will rain or snow" means "no rain, and no snow": denying an OR denies every
part of it. "It is not true that both the doors are locked" means "at least one door is unlocked":
denying an AND only needs one part to fail. That is De Morgan's law in words. A NOT pushed inside a
bracket flips every literal it meets and swaps OR with AND on the way in.

Why does the rule work? Apply De Morgan at the root: the complement of a product is the sum of the
complements of its factors. Each factor is itself a sum, so its complement is a product of
complements, and so on down to the leaves, where the complement is just a primed or unprimed
literal. Every operator is swapped exactly once and every literal is complemented exactly once.

attrs.title: A rule that is already covered by two other rules

c:
A shop rule says: members (x) who brought a coupon (y) get a discount; non-members (x′) who spend over
a limit (z) also get one. Someone suggests a third rule: anyone with a coupon who spends over the
limit (yz) gets a discount. It adds nothing. Such a customer is either a member (and has a coupon, so
rule 1 applies) or a non-member (and spent over the limit, so rule 2 applies). Whatever x is, one of
the two old rules already covers them. That redundant third rule is the consensus term.

attrs.title: Ask one question, then deal with the two cases

c:
A complicated rule often becomes simple once one fact is known. "Is the customer a member?" If yes,
the rule is one thing; if no, it is another. Shannon's expansion does exactly this to a Boolean
function: pick one variable, write down what the function becomes when that variable is 0 and when it
is 1, and glue the two answers together with the variable as the selector. Repeating it on every
variable gives a decision tree, which is how a multiplexer computes any function.

Any function can be split on one of its variables into "what it does when the variable is 0" and
"what it does when it is 1". This is the most general simplification tool there is, and it is also
the idea behind multiplexers (Chapter 5).

attrs.title: Each equation crosses out some rows

c:
A system of Boolean equations is a sieve. Start with every possible assignment of the variables; each
equation crosses out the rows on which its two sides differ; the rows that survive every equation are
the solutions. Because a sum is 0 only when every term is 0, equations of the form "sum = 0" cross out
most rows at once, so start with them.

A Boolean equation is solved by finding the input values that make it true. GATE has asked for the
solution of small systems three times; the method uses two facts and a little bookkeeping.

c:
XOR is the odd one out among the gates. It has no controlling value, it does not obey absorption,
and yet it has an algebra of its own that is

like school algebra than Boolean algebra is: you
can cancel, you can "move terms across", and a chain of XORs simply counts. This lesson builds that
algebra, applies it to parity, and then turns to the GATE favourite of defining a strange operator
by a formula or a table and asking whether it is commutative or associative, or what a nested
expression simplifies to. Sixteen previous-year questions live here.

attrs.title: Does the order of the ingredients matter?

c:
Mixing flour and sugar gives the same bowl whichever goes in first: that is commutativity. Mixing
flour with sugar and then adding eggs gives the same batter as mixing sugar with eggs and then adding
flour: that is associativity. Some kitchen operations fail one or both tests (you cannot "un-bake").
For a Boolean operator both questions are decided by its table: commutativity by two rows, associativity
by eight.

attrs.title: Why one gate can be enough

c:
Lesson 4 showed that every function is an OR of minterms, and a minterm is an AND of literals. So
three gates, AND, OR and NOT, are enough for everything. Now notice that you do not even need all
three: De Morgan turns an OR into an AND with inverted inputs and output, so AND and NOT suffice.
Push one step further. A NAND is an AND with a NOT built in, and a NAND with its inputs tied is a NOT.
So a NAND can play both roles, and NAND alone is enough.

The same chain of reasoning answers the general question "is this set of gates enough?". Try to build
NOT and AND (or NOT and OR) from it. If you can, it is complete. If you can't, there is always a
reason, and Post's theorem lists the only five possible reasons.

attrs.title: Five traps a set of gates can be stuck in

c:
Some gate sets cannot build everything, and every failure has a reason you can name. Gates that output
0 on all-zero inputs can never make anything else on all-zero inputs. Gates without any inversion can
never make NOT. Gates that are pure XORs can only ever make XORs. Each such reason is a "trap": a family
of functions closed under wiring, so a circuit built from members never leaves it. Post proved that
there are exactly five such traps that matter, and that a set of gates is complete exactly when it is
not caught in any of them.

(an XOR of some inputs and possibly 1).

attrs.title: Further depth: why NAND wins in silicon

c:
In CMOS a 2-input NAND puts its two series transistors in the fast NMOS pull-down network, while a NOR
puts them in the slower PMOS pull-up. So for equal drive strength a NAND needs smaller transistors than
a NOR, which makes it smaller and faster; that is why CMOS standard-cell libraries are built around NAND.
(The older TTL family was also NAND-based, for a different reason: its multi-emitter input transistor
naturally forms a NAND.)

attrs.title: A circuit is a recipe read from left to right

c:
A combinational circuit has no memory and no loops: every gate's inputs come from the circuit's inputs
or from gates further left. So you can always read it like a recipe. Name each intermediate result,
write each step in terms of earlier ones, and at the end substitute everything into the last step.
That is all "analysis" means.

What makes GATE circuits look hard is only notation: NAND and NOR gates stacked several levels deep
hide simple functions behind double negations, and function blocks hide them behind lists of numbers.
The tools for both are already in your hands: De Morgan cancels the negations, and set algebra
handles the lists.

attrs.title: News travels at a finite speed

c:
When an input changes, the news does not reach the output at once: each gate passes it on after a short
delay. If the news travels along two paths of different lengths and the paths meet again at a gate,
that gate briefly sees the new value on one input and the old value on the other. For that moment it
can compute something the truth table never allows: a short wrong pulse, a glitch. Timing questions are
about exactly these moments.

attrs.title: When every step changes the answer

c:
Parity flips whenever any input flips. On a map every step to a neighbour flips one input, so a parity
function alternates 1, 0, 1, 0 in every direction: a checkerboard, with no two 1s side by side and nothing
to loop. If only some inputs matter, the alternation happens only along those directions and the other
directions repeat, which leaves loops: an XOR or XNOR of fewer variables.

attrs.name: The checkerboard is parity

literals each). The same holds for even parity (XNOR).
a step to a neighbour flips one bit, and flipping one bit flips the parity.

The idea: covering a floor with rugs

Think of the 1-cells of a map as a floor you must cover with rectangular rugs. A rug may only lie on
floor (on 1s, never on 0s), and rugs come only in the legal K-map shapes. Big rugs are cheap (few
literals), small rugs are expensive. Overlapping is allowed.

Three observations solve the puzzle. First, never buy a rug that could be enlarged: a bigger rug in
the same place covers at least as much for less. Those maximal rugs are the

.
Second, if some spot of floor fits under only one maximal rug, that rug must be bought: it is

. Third, after buying the essential rugs, cover what is left as cheaply as you can; if
two choices cost the same, there are two equally good answers. Don't-cares are spots of floor you may
cover or leave bare, whichever is convenient.

attrs.title: Further depth: how many prime implicants can a function have?

c:
A search over all 256 functions of three variables finds at most 6 prime implicants (reached by the
cyclic

), and a search over all 65 536 functions of four variables finds at most
13 (reached, for example, by

). The maximum keeps growing
exponentially with

is hard for large functions and why design tools switch to heuristics for many inputs. For GATE-sized
maps, listing prime implicants by hand stays easy.

The idea: let a list do what the eye did

On a map you merged two neighbouring cells by seeing that they touch. In binary, two minterms touch
exactly when their patterns differ in one bit: 0101 and 0111 differ only in the third bit, so they
merge into 01-1 (the dash marks the variable that disappears). Two such dashed patterns merge again if
their dashes line up and they differ in one more bit: 01-1 and 11-1 give -1-1. Doing this
systematically, round after round, finds every loop you could have drawn, and a pattern that never
merges is a loop that cannot grow: a prime implicant. No geometry is needed, so the method works for
any number of variables.

attrs.title: Further depth: why exact minimisation gets hard

c:
Choosing the cheapest set of rows that covers every column is the set-cover problem, which is
NP-hard in general, and the number of prime implicants itself can grow exponentially with the number
of variables. Quine–McCluskey with Petrick's method is exact but can blow up; practical logic
minimisers work with heuristics (expand, reduce, irredundant passes) that usually reach a minimum or
come very close. For GATE-sized functions the exact method in this lesson is quick by hand.

A minimal expression is only useful once it is built. This lesson measures what "minimal" costs in

circuits, counts the fewest 2-input gates a function needs, and then meets a surprise: the cheapest
circuit can

when an input changes, and the cure is to add back a term that minimisation threw
away. Finally, circuits with several outputs can share product terms, which changes what "minimal"
means.

A two-level circuit is a row of AND gates feeding one OR gate (or ORs feeding an AND). Every literal is a
wire into an AND gate; every term is one AND gate and one wire into the OR gate. So fewer literals means
fewer wires, and fewer terms means fewer gates. A one-literal term needs no AND gate at all: the input
wire goes straight to the OR. Minimisation is simply buying the fewest boxes and wires that still
compute
the number of literal occurrences in the expression (
the number of product (or sum) terms.

for a two-level AND–OR circuit, one AND gate per term with at least two
literals plus one OR gate (if there are at least two terms); gate inputs = literals in the AND gates +
terms entering the OR gate.

"Minimal" in this chapter means fewest literals, then fewest terms. The measures usually agree; when
they do not, a question will say which one counts.

Until now we have been given functions: a minterm list, a map, an expression, a circuit to analyse.
Real design starts one step earlier, with a sentence: "light the lamp when at least two of the three
judges press their buttons", "convert a decimal digit to its excess-3 code", "output the digit modulo
six". This lesson turns such sentences into circuits by one fixed procedure (name the signals, write
the truth table, mark the rows that cannot happen as don't-cares, minimise each output, draw the
gates, check). We then count gates honestly and prove when a count is the minimum, and finish with the
most common family of design questions in GATE:

, circuits whose input is a word in
one code and whose output is the same value in another code.

attrs.title: A vending machine with no memory for coins

c: Imagine a vending machine that has no coin box: it looks only at which buttons are pressed

and drops the item that matches. Press the same buttons tomorrow and you get the same item; the
machine has no idea what was pressed a minute ago. That is a combinational circuit. Its output is a
fixed function of its present inputs, so a truth table describes it completely.

A real vending machine is different: it remembers how much money you have inserted, and the same
button gives "insert more coins" or a chocolate bar depending on that history. Remembering needs

loops are sequential circuits (Chapter 6). Everything in this chapter is loop-free, and that single
fact is what lets us design with truth tables and K-maps.

attrs.title: Every sentence is a set of rows

c:
A specification sentence is a filter on rows. "At least two inputs are 1" picks the rows with two or

select", the truth table writes itself, and the opposite question, "which expression does this table
represent", becomes "which expression is 1 on exactly these rows".

attrs.title: A fork in the road, decided by a sign

c:
A traveller reaches a fork with a sign: "if the bridge is open, take the left road, otherwise the
right". The traveller does not remember earlier signs and does not wait; the moment the sign changes, the
choice changes. A 2:1 MUX is that fork: the condition is the select line, the two roads are the two data
inputs. So whenever a specification or a piece of code reads "if … then this, else that", with both
branches producing a value from the present inputs, the hardware is a MUX.

MUX trees: big multiplexers from small ones

Sixteen players, and the courts hold four at a time. Round one: four groups of four, one winner each.
Round two: the four winners play once more. Five matches, two rounds, one champion. A MUX tree is the
same tournament: first-level MUXes each pick one candidate from their group of inputs, and the next
level picks among the winners. The least significant select bits decide the winner inside each
group; the most significant bits decide which group's winner reaches the output.

That is an active-low decoder. Its selected output is the one that is 0. Because every output is now the
complement of a minterm, the gate that collects them must change too: where an active-high decoder needs
an OR ("is any of my lamps lit?"), an active-low one needs a NAND ("is any of my lamps dark?"). The rest
of this block makes that precise.

c:
Some printed questions draw an AND gate on decoder outputs and expect you to read off a product of
maxterms, without ever saying that the outputs are active-low. Read literally, with ordinary active-high
outputs, an AND of two or more

outputs is the constant 0: two different minterms are never 1
on the same row. The same mix-up runs the other way: an OR of two or more different active-low outputs
is the constant 1, enabled or not: while enabled at most one of them can be 0, and while disabled every
one of them is 1.

So the first thing to settle for any decoder-plus-gate circuit is the output polarity. If the figure has
bubbles or the text says "active-low", outputs are maxterms; otherwise they are minterms. Examiners expect
two wrong answers here: "constant 0 / constant 1" from a student who assumed the wrong polarity, and the

from a student who used the right minterms with the wrong gate. In our own
questions we always state the polarity; when you meet an unstated AND-on-decoder question, say which
reading you used.

In a priority encoder the top-ranked inputs are the powerful ones: if the highest input is active, the

attrs.title: Count the rows, count the columns

Because a ROM stores the whole truth table, its size is the size of the table. The table has one row
for every combination of the inputs and one column for every output. Nothing else matters: not how

ROM is two counts. How many input bits form the address? That gives the number of words. How many
output bits does each row need? That gives the word width.

A circuit that has been designed correctly can still be built wrongly. A wire can be broken, a
transistor can be shorted, a gate output can be welded to the supply rail. When a chip comes off the
production line, nobody can open it and look; all a tester can do is apply input patterns and watch the
outputs. This lesson asks the testing questions GATE asks: what does a broken wire do to the logic,
how many different breakages are possible, which input pattern exposes a given breakage, and why some
breakages can never be seen at all. The answers rest on one simple model, the

, and
one simple idea: a fault is visible only if an input

broken copy, and compared. The rules for getting a signal through a gate use the

the redundant consensus term that

Imagine a light switch on the wall that is jammed in the ON position. You walk past it every day with
the lamp on and notice nothing, because the lamp is on exactly when you want it on. You discover the
fault only on the evening you try to switch the lamp

and it refuses. Two things had to happen:
you had to try to set the switch to the value it is stuck away from, and you had to be looking at a lamp
that actually depends on that switch. If the lamp were also wired through a second switch that happened
to be open, you would see darkness either way and learn nothing.

That is the whole of testing in one picture. A stuck line shows itself only when the input tries to
drive it to the other value (we call this

), and only if the rest of the circuit lets that
line decide the output (we call this

). Everything in this lesson is a careful version of
those two sentences.

used to generate tests in practice, because it is simple and because tests for single faults catch most

Two consequences matter in practice. First, undetectable faults are a sign of wasted logic. Removing the

sometimes added on purpose, for example the consensus term that removes a static hazard, and an
undetectable fault on it can sit there unnoticed and later mask another fault, or bring the hazard back.

absorption.title: Absorption and the loss of associativity
absorption.intro: A toy format with 4 fraction bits: x = 32 = 1.0000 × 2⁵ and y = 1 = 1.0000 × 2⁰. The next float above 32 is 34 (ulp = 2).

elements.text: Absorption: a small number added to a large one (4 fraction bits)
ulp(32) = 2 here, so half an ulp is 1

steps.caption: Align y to x's exponent 5: shift its significand right 5 places. The 1 lands just past the 4 kept bits: 0.0000 with guard bit 1 and round bit 0.
The extra bits are exactly half an ulp (G = 1, R = S = 0): a tie. Ties go to the even neighbour, and 1.0000 is even, so x + y rounds to 32. y has been absorbed.
Add 1 again: the same thing happens, so (32 + 1) + 1 = 32.
Now add the small numbers first: 1 + 1 = 2 exactly. Aligning 2 = 1.0000 × 2¹ to exponent 5 shifts it 4 places: 0.0001, with nothing left over. 32 + 2 = 1.0001 × 2⁵ = 34 exactly.
So (32 + 1) + 1 ≠ 32 + (1 + 1): floating-point addition is not associative. Adding the small terms first keeps them from being absorbed.

set.text: order matters: add small numbers first

adder-converter.title: The 1996 adder-based converter for three inputs
adder-converter.intro: A 4-bit adder adds b and the operand 0, b3·b2, 0, 0 with carry in 0; d4 is the carry out. The AND gate is the detector for b ≥ 12.

elements.text: GATE 1996's converter: add 0100 when b3 b2 = 11

steps.caption: The second operand is 0, b3·b2, 0, 0: it is 0100 (4) exactly when b3 = b2 = 1, i.e. b ≥ 12, and 0000 otherwise.
b = 1011 (11): b3·b2 = 0, so the adder adds 0. Output 0 1011: 0 twelve and 11 units = 11.
b = 1100 (12): b3·b2 = 1, so the adder adds 4. Output 1 0000: 1 twelve and 0 units = 12.
b = 1111 (15): b3·b2 = 1, so the adder adds 4. Output 1 0011: 1 twelve and 3 units = 15.
Units stay 0 … 11 and d4 counts twelves: binary to radix 12. A BCD converter would instead add 0110 from b = 10 up.

address-decoding.title: A 2-to-4 decoder selecting one of four 1 KB memory chips
address-decoding.intro: A 4 KB memory from four 1 KB chips. The 12-bit address A11…A0 splits: A11 A10 go to a 2:4 decoder that enables one chip; A9…A0 go to all chips.

elements.text: Address decoding: a 2:4 decoder picks one of four 1 KB chips

steps.caption: Each 1 KB chip needs 10 address lines (2¹⁰ = 1024): A9…A0 go to every chip. A11 A10 drive a 2:4 decoder whose outputs are chip selects.
0x000: A11 A10 = 00 raises Y0, selecting chip 0 (0x000–0x3FF); A9…A0 = 0x000 picks the byte in it.
0x5A3: A11 A10 = 01 raises Y1, selecting chip 1 (0x400–0x7FF); A9…A0 = 0x1A3 picks the byte in it.
0x800: A11 A10 = 10 raises Y2, selecting chip 2 (0x800–0xBFF); A9…A0 = 0x000 picks the byte in it.
0xFFF: A11 A10 = 11 raises Y3, selecting chip 3 (0xC00–0xFFF); A9…A0 = 0x3FF picks the byte in it.
Chip k holds addresses k·0x400 to k·0x400 + 0x3FF: the top two bits pick the chip, the low ten the byte. 4 × 1 KB = 4 KB.

addsub-overflow.title: A 4-bit adder–subtractor with its overflow detector
addsub-overflow.intro: Each b_i passes through an XOR with the control line K before entering the full adders; K is also the carry in c0. An XOR of c4 and c3 gives the overflow flag V.

elements.text: A 4-bit adder–subtractor: K inverts B and adds 1

steps.caption: K = 0: each XOR passes b_i unchanged (b ⊕ 0 = b) and the carry in c0 = K = 0, so the circuit is an ordinary adder.
K = 1: each XOR inverts its bit (b ⊕ 1 = b′) and c0 = 1 adds one: A + B′ + 1 = A − B in two's complement.
5 + 6: K = 0, sum 1011. c4 = 0 and c3 = 1 differ, so V = 1: 5 + 6 = 11 is outside −8 … 7.
−8 − 1: K = 1, sum 0111. c4 = 1 and c3 = 0 differ, so V = 1: −8 − 1 = -9 is outside −8 … 7.

alu-slice.title: A 4-bit ALU choosing among AND, OR, XOR and the adder–subtractor
alu-slice.intro: Four units compute AND, OR, XOR and ADD/SUB of A = 0110 and B = 0011 in parallel; a 4:1 MUX driven by F1F0 picks one result, and the flags are read from it.

elements.text: A 4-bit ALU: four results, one 4:1 MUX, the flags

steps.caption: All four units work on A and B at once; the function bits F1F0 only choose which result the MUX passes to Y.
F1F0 = 11, K = 0: Y = ADD(A, B) = 1001. V = 1: 6 + 3 = 9 overflows 4-bit two's complement.
F1F0 = 11, K = 1: Y = SUB(A, B) = 0011. K = 1 turns the adder into A − B: 3, C = 1 (no borrow).

arithmetic-shift.title: Arithmetic and logical shifts
arithmetic-shift.intro: The 8-bit pattern of −7, 11111001. Shifted copies will appear underneath.

steps.caption: Arithmetic shift right: every bit moves one place right, the last bit falls off, and the sign bit is copied into the empty top place. 11111001 → 11111100 = −4.
−7 ÷ 2 = −3.5, and the shift gave −4: an arithmetic right shift divides by 2 and rounds down (towards −∞), not towards zero.
A logical shift right fills the top with 0 instead. 01111100 = 124: fine for unsigned numbers, wrong for negative ones.
Shift left (arithmetic and logical are the same): a 0 enters at the right. 11110010 = −14 = 2 × (−7). It is exact because the top two bits of x were equal, so no significant bit was lost.

array-multiplier-grid.title: The critical path through a 4 × 4 array multiplier
array-multiplier-grid.intro: Three rows of four full-adder cells, shifted one bit per row. Partial products feed every cell; sums go down, carries go left. The product bits P0 … P7 leave at the right and the bottom.

elements.text: A 4 × 4 array multiplier and its critical path
16 AND gates make every partial product a_j b_i at t = 1

steps.caption: t = 1: all 16 partial products a_j·b_i are ready at once (one AND level). Row i of adders adds row i of them to the running sum.
t = 4: the carry ripples along row 1: cell (row 1, bit 0) is done.
t = 6: the carry moves left inside row 1: cell (row 1, bit 1) is done.
t = 8: the carry moves left inside row 1: cell (row 1, bit 2) is done.
t = 9: cell (row 1, bit 3) passes its sum down to the next row (same weight, one row lower).
t = 12: the carry moves left inside row 2: cell (row 2, bit 2) is done.
t = 13: cell (row 2, bit 3) passes its sum down to the next row (same weight, one row lower).
t = 16: the carry moves left inside row 3: cell (row 3, bit 2) is done.
t = 18: the last carry leaves cell (row 3, bit 3) as P7. Critical path: 8 cells, 18 gate delays = 6(n − 1).
The path only moves left (a carry) or down (a sum), never back: 8 cells here, O(n) in general, so Θ(n) delay with n² cells.

assoc-test.title: The associativity test for NAND
assoc-test.intro: To test whether an operator is associative, compare (a ⋆ b) ⋆ c with a ⋆ (b ⋆ c) on every row.

elements.text: Is NAND associative? Compare both bracketings on all 8 rows

steps.caption: Fill the column (a↑b)↑c: first NAND a with b, then NAND the result with c. Algebraically it is ab + c′.
Fill the column a↑(b↑c): it is a′ + bc.
The columns disagree on rows 001, 011, 100, 110. One disagreeing row is enough: NAND is not associative.
The same 8-row test works for any operator defined by a table: compute both bracketings and compare. AND, OR, XOR and XNOR pass it; NAND, NOR and implication fail.

base-carry-column.title: Column addition in base 8
base-carry-column.intro: Two octal numbers lined up by place: 37 above 45. Carries will appear above the columns.

elements.text: Adding (37)₈ + (45)₈: a column that reaches 8 carries

steps.caption: Units column: 7 + 5 = 12. In base 8, twelve is one eight and four units, so write 4 and carry 1 into the eights column.
Eights column: 3 + 4 + the carry 1 = 8. That is exactly one 64 and no eights, so write 0 and carry 1 again.
Nothing is left to add except the carry, so it becomes the leading digit: (37)₈ + (45)₈ = (104)₈.
Check in decimal: 31 + 37 = 68, and (104)₈ = 64 + 4 = 68.

bcd-adder-hw.title: A one-digit BCD adder with its correction detector
bcd-adder-hw.intro: Two 4-bit binary adders. The first adds the digits; a detector C4 + Z3Z2 + Z3Z1 decides whether the sum exceeds 9; the second adds 0110 when it does. The detector's output is the decimal carry.

elements.text: The BCD adder: add in binary, detect > 9, add 0110

steps.caption: Stage 1: an ordinary 4-bit adder adds the two BCD digits and the carry in. Its result C4 Z3 Z2 Z1 Z0 can be 0 … 19.
The detector fires when that binary sum is 10 or more: C4 = 1 (16–19) or Z = 1010 … 1111 (Z3Z2 or Z3Z1).
8 + 7 = 15: adder 1 gives 0 1111. Z = 1111 = 15 is not a BCD digit (Z3 = 1 with Z2 or Z1). Out: carry 1, digit 5.
4 + 5 = 9: adder 1 gives 0 1001. 1001 = 9 is a valid digit, so nothing is added. Out: carry 0, digit 9.
9 + 9 + 1 = 19: adder 1 gives 1 0011. C4 = 1 (sum 19 > 15) though Z = 0011 looks valid: only C4 catches it. Out: carry 1, digit 9.
8 + 9 = 17: adder 1 gives 1 0001. C4 = 1 (sum 17 > 15) though Z = 0001 looks valid: only C4 catches it. Out: carry 1, digit 7.

bcd-plus-six.title: BCD addition and the +6 correction
bcd-plus-six.intro: 386 and 457 in BCD, one 4-bit group per decimal digit. We add digit by digit from the right.

steps.caption: Units: 6 + 7 = 13 > 9, so add 0110: 1101 + 110 = 1 0011. Digit 3, decimal carry 1.
Tens: 8 + 5 + carry 1 = 14 > 9, so add 0110: 1110 + 110 = 1 0100. Digit 4, decimal carry 1.
Hundreds: 3 + 4 + carry 1 = 8, not above 9: no correction.
The result 1000 0100 0011 is BCD 843 = 386 + 457. Each +6 skipped the six unused patterns 1010 … 1111, so the carry came out at ten.

bcd-vs-binary.title: BCD versus binary
bcd-vs-binary.intro: Top: 59 in BCD, two 4-bit groups 0101 (5) and 1001 (9), each with weights 8 4 2 1. Bottom: 59 in pure binary, 111011, six bits with weights 32 to 1. BCD spends 8 bits where binary needs 6, and reading the BCD pattern as plain binary gives 89.

elements.text: 59 in BCD and in pure binary
read as binary, the BCD pattern 0101 1001 would be 89, not 59

bias-order.title: Biased exponents keep the unsigned order
bias-order.intro: Eight 3-bit exponent fields with their unsigned value, their 2's-complement value, and their value in excess-4 and excess-3.

elements.text: A 3-bit exponent field read in three codes
Unsigned order runs top to bottom.

steps.caption: The fields 000 … 111 are listed in unsigned order, top to bottom. A comparator that reads them as unsigned numbers puts each row above the one before it.
Read as 2's complement, the order breaks between 011 (+3) and 100 (−4): the bigger field holds the smaller exponent. A float with exponent −1 (111) would compare above one with exponent +3 (011).
Excess-4 (bias 2³⁻¹ = 4) subtracts 4 from the unsigned value: −4, −3, …, +3. The exponents now rise exactly as the fields rise.
Excess-3 (bias 2³⁻¹ − 1, the IEEE choice) gives −3 … +4, also in order. IEEE then reserves the end fields 000 and 111 for zero, denormals, infinity and NaN.

bitpair-table.title: Bit-pair recoding table
bitpair-table.intro: The eight multiplier triples and the radix-4 partial product each one selects.

steps.caption: Each radix-4 digit pairs two Booth digits: D = 2d(i+1) + d(i) = −2q(i+1) + q(i) + q(i−1). The eight triples give the digits 0, ±1, ±2.
So −29 = 0·4³ − 2·4² + 1·4 − 1: four radix-4 digits, at most four partial products for 8 bits, each a shift of ±M or ±2M.

block-sets.title: Unknown blocks in a circuit of functions, by minterm sets
block-sets.intro: Four-variable functions as rows 0–15. The circuit computes f = f₁·f₂ + f₃ with f₁ = Σ(1, 3, 5, 7, 9), f₂ = Σ(3, 7, 9, 12) and the target f = Σ(3, 7, 9, 14).

elements.text: Solving f = f₁·f₂ + f₃ for the unknown block

steps.caption: AND is intersection: f₁·f₂ = Σ(3, 7, 9). These rows are already supplied by the AND gate.
The target is f = Σ(3, 7, 9, 14). First check that f₁·f₂ lies inside f; it does, so a solution exists.
OR is union, so f₃ must supply every row of f that the AND does not: f₃ must contain row 14.
f₃ must also stay inside f (any extra row would appear in the output). So f₃ = Σ(14) plus any subset of {3, 7, 9}: f − f₁f₂ ⊆ f₃ ⊆ f.

booth-datapath.title: Booth multiplier datapath stepping through 6 × (−3)
booth-datapath.intro: Registers M (multiplicand), A (accumulator, one extra bit), Q (multiplier) and the bit Q−1. The control looks at Q0 Q−1 and tells the adder–subtractor to add M, subtract M or do nothing; then A, Q, Q−1 shift right together.

steps.caption: Start: A = 0 (5 bits: one extra bit so that −M always fits), Q = multiplier −3 = 1101, Q−1 = 0, M = 6.
Cycle 1: Q0 Q−1 = 10, so subtract M: A = 11010.
Cycle 1: arithmetic right shift of A, Q, Q−1 (A's sign bit is copied): A = 11101, Q = 0110, Q−1 = 1.
Cycle 2: Q0 Q−1 = 01, so add M: A = 00011.
Cycle 2: arithmetic right shift of A, Q, Q−1 (A's sign bit is copied): A = 00001, Q = 1011, Q−1 = 0.
Cycle 3: Q0 Q−1 = 10, so subtract M: A = 11011.
Cycle 3: arithmetic right shift of A, Q, Q−1 (A's sign bit is copied): A = 11101, Q = 1101, Q−1 = 1.
Cycle 4: Q0 Q−1 = 11, so no add: A = 11101.
Cycle 4: arithmetic right shift of A, Q, Q−1 (A's sign bit is copied): A = 11110, Q = 1110, Q−1 = 1.
After n = 4 cycles, A Q = 11101110 = −18 = 6 × (−3). One adder, n cycles, at most n additions or subtractions.

booth-scan.title: Booth recoding: a sliding pair window
booth-scan.intro: The 8-bit multiplier −29 = 11100011 with a 0 appended on the right (q₋₁). A window covers the current bit and the bit to its right.

elements.text: Booth recoding of −29 = 11100011: slide a 2-bit window

steps.caption: i = 0: the window holds (q0, q₋₁) = (1, 0), so d0 = 0 − 1 = −1 (a run of 1s starts here: subtract M).
i = 1: the window holds (q1, q0) = (1, 1), so d1 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
i = 2: the window holds (q2, q1) = (0, 1), so d2 = 1 − 0 = +1 (a run of 1s ended just below: add M).
i = 3: the window holds (q3, q2) = (0, 0), so d3 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
i = 4: the window holds (q4, q3) = (0, 0), so d4 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
i = 5: the window holds (q5, q4) = (1, 0), so d5 = 0 − 1 = −1 (a run of 1s starts here: subtract M).
i = 6: the window holds (q6, q5) = (1, 1), so d6 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
i = 7: the window holds (q7, q6) = (1, 1), so d7 = 0 (inside a run: shift only).
Read the digits MSB first: 0 0 −1 0 0 +1 0 −1 = −32 + 4 − 1 = −29. Three operations instead of five additions (one per 1): the run of three 1s at the top costs a single subtraction.

bubble-push.title: Bubble pushing turns NAND into a bubbled OR and NOR into a bubbled AND
bubble-push.intro: A NAND gate, drawn the usual way: an AND body with a bubble (inversion) on its output.

elements.text: Bubble pushing: De Morgan in pictures
NAND = AND with an output bubble

steps.caption: A NAND gate is an AND gate followed by NOT. Its output is 0 only when both inputs are 1: the column (AB)′ reads 1, 1, 1, 0.
Push the bubble backwards through the gate. Two things change: the body flips from AND to OR, and the one bubble splits into a bubble on every input.

set.text: the same gate drawn as an OR with bubbled inputs

steps.caption: Check it: A′ + B′ is 1 unless both A and B are 1, exactly the NAND column. This is De Morgan's law (AB)′ = A′ + B′.
The same move turns a NOR into an AND with bubbled inputs: (A + B)′ = A′B′. Both are 1 only on row 00.

set.text: NOR drawn as an AND with bubbled inputs

steps.caption: The rule: moving bubbles across a gate swaps AND and OR and complements every input and output it crosses. Two bubbles on one wire cancel.

carry-select.title: A carry-select adder choosing between two precomputed upper halves
carry-select.intro: An 8-bit carry-select adder: a lower 4-bit ripple adder, two upper 4-bit ripple adders (carry in 0 and carry in 1) and a row of 2:1 MUXes driven by the lower carry c4.

elements.text: Carry-select: compute the upper half both ways, then choose

steps.caption: t = 0: all three 4-bit ripple adders start at once. The upper half does not wait: it adds both ways, with carry in 0 and 1.
t = 9: the upper adders finish: 1001 (carry 0) and 1010 (carry 0).
t = 9 too: the lower adder gives 0001 with carry c4 = 1. Every adder took 2 × 4 + 1 = 9 gate delays.
t = 11: c4 = 1 selects the 'carry in 1' result through the MUX (2 gate levels): s7–4 = 1010, carry out 0.
Sum 10100001 = 107 + 54 = 161 after 11 gate delays; an 8-bit ripple adder needs 17. The price: a third adder and the MUXes.

circuit-read.title: Reading a three-gate circuit, one level at a time
circuit-read.intro: Three gates: G1 is a NAND of A and B, G2 an OR of B and C, and G3 an AND of the two results.

elements.text: Reading a circuit: label every gate, then follow the signals

steps.caption: Set the inputs A = 0, B = 1, C = 0. B feeds two gates (a fan-out), so it appears twice.
Level 2. F = AND(G1, G2) = 1·1 = 1. Every gate waited for its inputs: values flow left to right, one level at a time.
Set the inputs A = 1, B = 1, C = 0. B feeds two gates (a fan-out), so it appears twice.
Level 2. F = AND(G1, G2) = 0·1 = 0. Only G1 changed, and that was enough to change F.
Written as an expression, the circuit is F = (AB)′(B + C): G1 and G2 are the two factors, G3 multiplies them.

cla-gp-tree.title: A two-level carry look-ahead tree for a 16-bit adder
cla-gp-tree.intro: Sixteen bit pairs make p and g; four blocks make group G and P; a second-level unit makes the block carries; each block then makes its inner carries and sums.

elements.text: Two-level carry look-ahead for 16 bits: up the tree, then down
level 1: p_i = a_i ⊕ b_i, g_i = a_i b_i (bit 15 … 0)

elements.label: second-level lookahead: c4, c8, c12, c16

steps.caption: t = 1: every bit makes p_i = a_i ⊕ b_i and g_i = a_i b_i in one gate level, all 16 in parallel.
t = 2: each block's P = p3 p2 p1 p0 is one AND of its four p's.
t = 3: each block's G = g3 + p3g2 + p3p2g1 + p3p2p1g0 (AND then OR). Block 0's c1–c3 are ready too.
t = 4: c4 = G0 + P0·c0 from the second-level unit; the sums s0–s3 are done.
t = 5: c8, c12, c16 = G + PG + PPG + … over the blocks: the top of the tree is done; s4 is done.
t = 6: going down: block 1 makes c5–c7 from c4 in two levels; s8 and s12 are done.
t = 7: blocks 2 and 3 make c9–c11 and c13–c15 from c8 and c12; s5–s7 are done.
t = 8: the last sums s9–s11 and s13–s15 are done. 8 gate delays, against 33 for a ripple adder.

code-tables.title: Decimal digits in four codes
code-tables.intro: A table of the digits 0 to 9 in 8421 BCD, excess-3, 2421 and 4-bit Gray code. For example 5 is 0101 in BCD, 1000 in excess-3, 1011 in 2421 and 0111 in Gray; 9 is 1001, 1100, 1111 and 1101.

column-add-carry.title: Binary column addition with a moving carry
column-add-carry.intro: Two bytes, 181 and 110, written one above the other. The small row on top will hold the carries.

elements.text: Adding 10110101 + 01101110, one column at a time

steps.caption: Column 0: 1 + 0 = 1, which is 1 in binary: write 1, no carry.
Column 1: 0 + 1 = 1, which is 1 in binary: write 1, no carry.
Column 2: 1 + 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 3: 0 + 1 + carry 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 4: 1 + 0 + carry 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 5: 1 + 1 + carry 1 = 3, which is 11 in binary: write 1, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 6: 0 + 1 + carry 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
Column 7: 1 + 0 + carry 1 = 2, which is 10 in binary: write 0, carry 1 to the next column.
The carry out of column 7 becomes a ninth bit: the sum is 1 0010 0011 = 291 = 181 + 110. In an 8-bit register the 1 would be the carry flag.

comparator-cascade.title: A 4-bit magnitude comparator deciding from the most significant bit
comparator-cascade.intro: Two 4-bit numbers A and B are compared bit by bit. Each XNOR gives xᵢ = 1 when Aᵢ = Bᵢ. Outputs: G (A > B), E (A = B), L (A < B).

elements.text: Comparing two 4-bit numbers from the MSB down

steps.caption: A = 1011 (11), B = 1001 (9). Bit 3: A3 = B3 = 1, so x3 = 1 and the decision passes to the next lower bit.
Bit 2: A2 = B2 = 0, so x2 = 1 and the decision passes to the next lower bit.
Bit 1: A1 = 1, B1 = 0, the first unequal bit. The term x3 x2 A1B1′ = 1 fires, so G = 1: A > B (11 > 9). Bits below 1 are ignored.
A = 0110 and B = 0110: every bit pair is equal, so all four XNORs output 1.
x3·x2·x1·x0 = 1, so E = 1 and neither G nor L fires: A = B.
A = 0101 (5), B = 0111 (7). Bit 3: A3 = B3 = 0, so x3 = 1 and the decision passes to the next lower bit.
Bit 2: A2 = B2 = 1, so x2 = 1 and the decision passes to the next lower bit.
Bit 1: A1 = 0, B1 = 1, the first unequal bit. The term x3 x2 A1′B1 = 1 fires, so L = 1: A < B (5 < 7). Bits below 1 are ignored.
G = A3B3′ + x3A2B2′ + x3x2A1B1′ + x3x2x1A0B0′ (xᵢ = Aᵢ ⊙ Bᵢ); L swaps A and B; E = x3x2x1x0. The MSB decides unless it ties.

set.text: G, L: first unequal bit from the top

comparator-chain.title: Two 4-bit magnitude comparators cascaded into an 8-bit comparator
comparator-chain.intro: An 8-bit comparator from two 4-bit chips. Each chip has outputs G, E, L and cascade inputs; the low chip's outputs drive the high chip's cascade inputs.

elements.text: Two 4-bit comparators cascaded into an 8-bit comparator

steps.caption: The low chip compares bits 3–0 with cascade inputs G, E, L = 0, 1, 0; its G, E, L feed the high chip's cascade inputs.
A = 0x5A, B = 0x3F. Low chip: 1010 < 1111, so it sends L = 1 to the high chip's cascade inputs.
High chip: 0101 > 0011, the nibbles differ, so it outputs G = 1 and ignores its cascade inputs: 90 > 63.
A = 0x5A, B = 0x5C. Low chip: 1010 < 1100, so it sends L = 1 to the high chip's cascade inputs.
High chip: 0101 = 0101, a tie, so it passes its cascade inputs: L = 1, the low chip's verdict. 90 < 92.
A = 0x5A, B = 0x5A. Low chip: 1010 = 1010, so it sends E = 1 to the high chip's cascade inputs.
High chip: 0101 = 0101, a tie, so it passes its cascade inputs: E = 1, the low chip's verdict. 90 = 90.
The high chip decides unless its nibbles tie; then it copies the low chip's G, E, L. The lowest chip's cascade inputs are tied to 0, 1, 0.

set.text: more chips: chain them the same way

complement-subtraction.title: Complement subtraction with the end-around carry
complement-subtraction.intro: M = 1010100 (84). We will subtract N = 1000011 (67) using only an adder and bit inversion.

elements.text: 84 − 67 with the 1's complement and the end-around carry

steps.caption: Write N = 1000011 (67) and flip every bit: N̄ = 0111100. This is the 1's complement, 2⁷ − 1 − 67 = 60.
Add M + N̄ = 1010100 + 0111100 = 1 0010000. The sum is 144 = 2⁷ + 16: a carry comes out of the top bit because M > N.
End-around carry: remove the carry (worth 2⁷) and add it back as 1 at the bottom. Removing 2⁷ leaves M − N − 1 = 16; adding 1 corrects the 'one short' of the 1's complement.
Result 0010001 = 17 = 84 − 67. Had there been no carry, the result would have been negative, with magnitude equal to the 1's complement of the sum.

complement-tree.title: Complementing an expression: swap operators, complement literals
complement-tree.intro: The expression f = (A + B′C)(A′ + D) drawn as a tree: operators inside, literals at the leaves.

elements.text: Complement = swap every operator, complement every literal

steps.caption: General De Morgan, rule 1: swap every operator, AND ↔ OR. The root AND becomes an OR, the two ORs become ANDs, and the inner AND becomes an OR.
Rule 2: complement every literal. A becomes A′, B′ becomes B, C becomes C′, A′ becomes A and D becomes D′.
Read the new tree back, keeping its grouping: the root is now an OR, so f′ = A′(B + C′) + AD′. A truth table over all 16 rows confirms it is 1 exactly where f is 0.

completeness-checklist.title: Functional completeness by Post's five classes
completeness-checklist.intro: Each row is a set of gates; each column one of Post's five closed classes.

elements.text: Post's test: a set must escape all five classes
T0: 0-preserving · T1: 1-preserving · S: self-dual · M: monotone · A: affine. ✓ = some member is outside the class.

steps.caption: NAND escapes every class: NAND(0, 0) = 1, NAND(1, 1) = 0, it is not self-dual, not monotone (0 → 1 lowers it) and not affine. Complete on its own.
AND and OR are both monotone (and 0- and 1-preserving): they can never produce a complement. Not complete.
XOR and NOT are both affine (x ⊕ y and x ⊕ 1): every circuit of them is an XOR of inputs and constants. Not complete.
AND escapes the self-dual and affine classes, NOT escapes the preserving and monotone ones: together they escape all five. Complete.
Implication escapes everything except 1-preservation (1 → 1 = 1). Not complete alone; add the constant 0 and it is.
Majority is self-dual, monotone, 0- and 1-preserving. Not complete, even with free constants (constants are monotone).
The 2:1 MUX preserves 0 and 1, so alone it is not complete; with the constants 0 and 1 it is (it then makes NOT and AND).

consensus-cells.title: The consensus theorem on the rows of a truth table
consensus-cells.intro: Three product terms over x, y, z, each drawn as the set of rows where it is 1.

elements.text: Consensus: yz is already covered by xy and x′z

steps.caption: Each cell is one row xyz of the truth table. The term xy is 1 on rows 110 and 111.
The term x′z is 1 on rows 001 and 011.
The consensus term yz is 1 on rows 011 and 111. Row 111 is already in xy (there x = 1) and row 011 is already in x′z (there x = 0).
So adding yz adds no new 1: xy + x′z + yz = xy + x′z. Whatever x is, one of the first two terms already covers yz.

set.text: yz lies inside xy + x′z, so it is redundant

converter-kmaps.title: BCD to excess-3 converter: four K-maps with don't-cares
converter-kmaps.intro: Four K-maps over the BCD digit B3 B2 B1 B0, one per excess-3 output bit E3 E2 E1 E0 (the digit plus 3). Cells 0–9 hold the outputs; cells 10–15 are don't-cares X.

elements.text: BCD → excess-3: four K-maps with don't-cares

steps.caption: Rows 10–15 are not BCD digits, so every output has an X there: six don't-cares per map that a loop may use or ignore.
The MSB E3 is 1 for digits 5–9. The octet B3 uses the Xs; quads B2B1 and B2B0 take the other 1s. E3 = B3 + B2B1 + B2B0 (3 terms).
E2 is 1 for digits 1–4 and 9: quads B2′B1 and B2′B0 use Xs, pair B2B1′B0′ (cells 4, 12) takes 4. E2 = B2′B1 + B2′B0 + B2B1′B0′ (3 terms).
E1 = 1 when B1 = B0: the left column quad B1′B0′ and the third column quad B1B0. E1 = B1′B0′ + B1B0 (2 terms).
The LSB E0 is 1 for the even digits: the octet B0′ (two outer columns) covers them all. E0 = B0′ (1 term).
All four maps are done: 17 literals in all. Without the don't-cares every map would need more or larger terms.

cyclic-map.title: The cyclic function Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) and its two minimal covers
cyclic-map.intro: Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6) on a 3-variable map (rows A, columns B C).

elements.text: A cyclic function: no essential prime implicant

steps.caption: Σm(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6): every 1 except the corners of the cube 000 and 111. Each 1 has exactly two neighbouring 1s, so it can be looped in two different pairs.
The six pairs form a ring: 1–3, 3–2, 2–6, 6–4, 4–5, 5–1. All six are prime implicants and every 1 is in two of them, so no prime implicant is essential.
Pick every other pair around the ring: B′C + A′B + AC′. Three pairs, 6 literals, every 1 covered once.
Or start one step further round: A′C + BC′ + AB′. Also three pairs and 6 literals. Two different minimal SOPs: the minimal form is not unique.

decoder-function.title: A decoder and an OR gate implementing the full-adder sum
decoder-function.intro: A 3:8 decoder with inputs A, B, C. Its outputs D1, D2, D4 and D7 feed a 4-input OR gate whose output is S.

elements.text: Decoder + OR gate: the full-adder sum Σ(1, 2, 4, 7)

steps.caption: A B C = 000: the decoder raises D0. D0 is not wired to the OR, so S = 0.
A B C = 001: the decoder raises D1. D1 is wired to the OR, so S = 1.
A B C = 010: the decoder raises D2. D2 is wired to the OR, so S = 1.
A B C = 011: the decoder raises D3. D3 is not wired to the OR, so S = 0.
A B C = 100: the decoder raises D4. D4 is wired to the OR, so S = 1.
A B C = 101: the decoder raises D5. D5 is not wired to the OR, so S = 0.
A B C = 110: the decoder raises D6. D6 is not wired to the OR, so S = 0.
A B C = 111: the decoder raises D7. D7 is wired to the OR, so S = 1.
The OR collects minterms 1, 2, 4, 7: S = A ⊕ B ⊕ C, the full-adder sum. Any n-variable function is an n:2ⁿ decoder plus an OR.

decoder-lighting.title: A 3-to-8 decoder lighting one output per address
decoder-lighting.intro: A 3:8 decoder with address inputs A2 A1 A0, an enable EN, and outputs D0–D7 (active high). The address will step from 000 to 111.

elements.text: A 3:8 decoder: one output per address

steps.caption: Address A2A1A0 = 000 (= 0) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D0, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 001 (= 1) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D1, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 010 (= 2) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D2, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 011 (= 3) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D3, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 100 (= 4) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D4, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 101 (= 5) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D5, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 110 (= 6) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D6, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Address A2A1A0 = 111 (= 7) with EN = 1: exactly one output, D7, is 1; the other seven are 0.
Enable low: the address is 101 again, but EN = 0, so every output is 0. The enable gates all eight outputs.
EN back to 1: D5 lights again. Each output Dk is the minterm m_k of A2A1A0 ANDed with EN, so a decoder is a minterm generator.

decoder-tree.title: A 6-to-64 decoder built from 3-to-8 decoders
decoder-tree.intro: A 6:64 decoder must be built from 3:8 decoders that have an enable input. The address is A5…A0.

elements.text: A2 A1 A0 go to every leaf

steps.caption: Level 1: one 3:8 decoder takes the high address bits A5 A4 A3. Its eight outputs will not drive loads directly; they choose a leaf.
Level 2: 64 outputs need 64 / 8 = 8 leaf decoders. Each top output drives one leaf's enable, and the low bits A2 A1 A0 go to every leaf.
Count: 8 leaves + 1 top decoder = 9 decoders, and no other gates, because a 3:8 decoder has an enable input.
Address A5…A0 = 101 110: the top decoder enables leaf 5 only; that leaf decodes 110 = 6 and raises its output 6, D46.
Address A5…A0 = 000 011: the top decoder enables leaf 0 only; that leaf decodes 011 = 3 and raises its output 3, D3.
In general an n:2ⁿ decoder from k:2ᵏ decoders needs 2ⁿ / 2ᵏ leaves plus the tree above them; for 6:64 from 3:8 that is 8 + 1 = 9.

delay-models.title: The 2015 ripple adder timed under the block model and at gate level
delay-models.intro: Two timelines in microseconds for a 4-bit ripple adder with XOR = 2.4 µs and AND = OR = 1.2 µs: the top one counts each full adder as a 4.8 µs block, the bottom one follows the carries gate by gate.

elements.text: GATE 2015: block model vs gate level (µs)
block model: each FA waits for the previous one
gate level: after FA0 a carry needs only AND + OR

steps.caption: One full adder: sum = XOR + XOR = 4.8 µs, carry = XOR + AND + OR = 4.8 µs. In the block model FA0 occupies 0 … 4.8.
Block model: FA1 starts only when FA0 has finished, at 4.8 µs, and ends at 9.6.
Block model: FA2 starts only when FA1 has finished, at 9.6 µs, and ends at 14.4.
Block model: FA3 starts only when FA2 has finished, at 14.4 µs, and ends at 19.2.
Block model total: 4 × 4.8 = 19.2 µs, the official key of GATE 2015.
Gate level: c1 still needs XOR + AND + OR = 4.8 µs, because p0 = a0 ⊕ b0 must be ready first.
But p1, p2, p3 were made in parallel long ago, so each later carry costs only AND + OR = 2.4 µs: c2 at 7.2, c3 at 9.6, c4 at 12.
The last sum s3 = p3 ⊕ c3 is ready at 9.6 + 2.4 = 12 µs too. Gate level: 12 µs; block model: 19.2 µs.

set.text: gate level 12 µs vs block model 19.2 µs

demux-routing.title: A 1-to-4 demultiplexer routing the data bit
demux-routing.intro: A 1:4 DEMUX: one data input D, select lines S1 S0, and outputs Y0–Y3. The selects choose which output receives D.

elements.text: A 1:4 DEMUX sends D to the selected output

steps.caption: S1S0 = 00, D = 1: the data bit travels to Y0, so Y0 = 1 and the other outputs are 0.
S1S0 = 01, D = 1: the data bit travels to Y1, so Y1 = 1 and the other outputs are 0.
S1S0 = 10, D = 1: the data bit travels to Y2, so Y2 = 1 and the other outputs are 0.
S1S0 = 11, D = 1: the data bit travels to Y3, so Y3 = 1 and the other outputs are 0.
S1S0 = 10, D = 0: the path still leads to Y2, but it carries 0, so every output is 0.
Each output is Yk = D · m_k(S1, S0). That is a 2:4 decoder whose enable is the data line: the same chip serves as decoder or DEMUX.

design-pipeline.title: Design procedure: a word specification becomes a 3-gate circuit
design-pipeline.intro: The specification: a 4-bit BCD digit ABCD enters, and F must be 1 when the digit is 5 or more. Four stages follow: truth table, K-map, expression, circuit.

elements.text: Design procedure: “BCD digit ≥ 5” from words to gates

steps.caption: Stage 1, the truth table: F = 1 for digits 5–9, F = 0 for 0–4; the codes 1010–1111 never occur in BCD, so their F is a don't-care X.
Stage 2, the K-map: the five 1s (cells 5–9) and the six Xs (cells 10–15) are copied into a 4-variable map in Gray order.
Stage 3, grouping: the Xs let the 1s at 8 and 9 join cells 10–15 in an octet, the whole A = 1 half of the map, which reads A.
Two quads finish the cover: BC (cells 6, 7, 14, 15) and BD (cells 5, 7, 13, 15). Minimal SOP: F = A + BC + BD = A + B(C + D).
Stage 4: three gates, OR(C, D), AND with B, OR with A. No AND/OR/NOT circuit with fewer gates exists.
Test digit 6 = 0110: C + D = 1, B(C + D) = 1, so F = 1, as the table says (6 ≥ 5).
Test digit 3 = 0011: C + D = 1 but B = 0, so B(C + D) = 0 and A = 0, so F = 0 (3 < 5).

dont-care-toggle.title: Using don't-cares only where they enlarge a loop
dont-care-toggle.intro: Σm(1, 3, 7, 11, 15) + d(0, 5) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D); X marks a don't-care.

elements.text: Don't-cares: use an X only if it makes a loop bigger
Use an X only if it helps

steps.caption: f = Σm(1, 3, 7, 11, 15) + d(0, 5). The X cells may be treated as 1 or as 0, whichever gives the cheaper expression; they never need to be covered.
Column C D = 11 (m3, m7, m15, m11) is a quad of 1s: CD.
m1 is left. Without don't-cares its best loop is the pair m1, m3: A′B′D, 3 literals.
Treat X at m5 as 1: m1, m3, m5, m7 become a quad, A′D, with only 2 literals. The X at m0 would not enlarge any loop, so it stays 0 and is left out.

doubling-peel.title: Repeated doubling: 0.625 to binary
doubling-peel.intro: We will double the fraction again and again. Each integer part that pops out is one bit after the point.

elements.text: 0.625 to binary: double, peel off the integer part

steps.caption: 0.625 × 2 = 1.25. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.25 for the next round.
0.25 × 2 = 0.5. The integer part 0 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0.5 for the next round.
0.5 × 2 = 1. The integer part 1 is the next bit after the point; keep the fraction 0 for the next round. The fraction left is 0, so the expansion stops: 0.625 has a finite binary form.
The bits come out first-to-last from the top, so read the column downward: 0.625 = (0.101)₂ = 1/2 + 1/8.

epi-highlight.title: Essential prime implicants from the 1s covered only once
epi-highlight.intro: Σm(1, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14) on a 4-variable map (rows A B, columns C D).

elements.text: Essential prime implicants: 1s with only one way out

steps.caption: f = Σm(1, 3, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 14) has 7 prime implicants. Count, for every 1-cell, how many of them contain it.
Three 1s lie in exactly one prime implicant: m1, m10 and m13 (shaded). Any cover must use that implicant, so it is essential.
The essential prime implicants: A′B′D, ACD′, ABC′. Draw them first.
Still uncovered: m6 and m7. Of the remaining prime implicants, A′BC covers both; A′CD or BCD′ would cover only one each and need a second term. So A′BC is the cheapest way to finish.
Minimal SOP: f = A′B′D + A′BC + ACD′ + ABC′. ABD′ is redundant: its 1s are all inside the essential ones.

equality-xnor.title: A 4-bit equality comparator from XNOR gates and an AND gate
equality-xnor.intro: Two 4-bit numbers A and B. Each bit pair goes to an XNOR gate; the four XNOR outputs go to a 4-input AND, whose output E is 1 when A = B.

elements.text: 4-bit equality: four XNORs and an AND

steps.caption: Each XNOR gives xᵢ = Aᵢ ⊙ Bᵢ, which is 1 exactly when the two bits are equal. The AND gives E = x3x2x1x0.
A = 1011, B = 1011: every pair is equal, so x3x2x1x0 = 1111 and the AND gives E = 1.
A = 1011, B = 1001: only bit 1 differs, so x1 = 0 and E = 0. One unequal pair is enough.
A = 0110, B = 1001: every pair differs, x3x2x1x0 = 0000, so E = 0.
E = (A3 ⊙ B3)(A2 ⊙ B2)(A1 ⊙ B1)(A0 ⊙ B0): n XNORs and one n-input AND test n-bit equality.

equation-sieve.title: A system of Boolean equations solved by elimination
equation-sieve.intro: All 16 assignments of P, Q, R, S (row PQRS). Each equation keeps only the rows on which its two sides are equal.

elements.text: Solving a system by striking out rows

steps.caption: Equation: P + Q = 1. At least one of P, Q is 1: the four rows with P = Q = 0 go. Twelve rows survive.
Equation: PQ = 0. P and Q are not both 1: the four rows with P = Q = 1 go. Exactly one of P, Q is 1 on the eight survivors.
Equation: Q + R = R. Q + R = R means Q = 1 forces R = 1: rows 0100 and 0101 go. Six rows survive.
Equation: P′R + S = 0. A sum equal to 0: S = 0, and P = 0 forces R = 0, which kills the remaining P = 0 rows. Two rows survive: PQRS = 1000 and 1010.

excess3-correction.title: Excess-3 addition and its ±3 correction
excess3-correction.intro: 47 and 38 in excess-3 (each digit plus 3, in 4 bits).

elements.text: Excess-3 addition 47 + 38: −3 without a carry, +3 with one

steps.caption: Units: 1010 + 1011 = 1 0101. A carry came out, so the digit sum was 10 or more: add 3. 0101 + 0011 = 1000 (excess-3 of 5), decimal carry 1.
Tens: 0111 + 0110 + carry 1 = 1110, with no carry out: the digit sum was at most 9, so subtract 3: 1110 − 0011 = 1011 (excess-3 of 8).
Why: each code carries an excess of 3, so a sum carries an excess of 6. Without a carry, remove 3 to leave a single excess of 3. With a carry, the 16 taken away already over-removed, so put 3 back.
Result 1011 1000 is excess-3 of 85 = 47 + 38.

fault-blocked.title: A stuck-at fault whose activation blocks its own propagation
fault-blocked.intro: X1 X2 X3 feed a 3-input NAND; its output and X4 feed an OR. T = AND(X3, X4). The OR output and T feed a NOR, the circuit output.

steps.caption: T = X3·X4 feeds the NOR. The fault: T stuck-at-0 (tied to ground). To activate it, the good T must be 1, so X3 = X4 = 1.
But X4 = 1 also enters the OR, and 1 is the OR's controlling value: o = 1 whatever the NAND gives, so the NOR output is 0.
X = 0 1 1 1: T = 1/0 is activated, but X4 = 1 makes o = 1, so out = 0/0 in both circuits.
X = 1 1 1 1: T = 1/0 is activated, but X4 = 1 makes o = 1, so out = 0/0 in both circuits.
X = 0 0 0 0: X3 = X4 = 0, so the good T is 0, the stuck value: not activated; out = 0/0. No test.
No input detects T s-a-0: activation (X4 = 1) blocks propagation. The answer is D, none of the above; T is redundant.

set.text: undetectable: T can be tied to 0

fault-injection.title: Injecting a stuck-at-1 fault and finding the test vector
fault-injection.intro: Two copies of the circuit p = (AB)′, f = (p·C)′. The lower copy has line p stuck at 1. Every input row is applied to both copies.

elements.text: Stuck-at-1 on line p (GATE 1994): which input detects it?

steps.caption: Rows 000–101 (A or B is 0): good p = (AB)′ = 1, the stuck value, so the fault is not activated; all 6 rows agree.
A B C = 1 1 0: good p = 0 differs from the stuck 1, but C = 0 forces f = 1 in both circuits, so nothing propagates.
A B C = 1 1 1: good p = 0, f = (0·1)′ = 1; faulty p = 1, f = (1·1)′ = 0. The outputs differ: a test.
Only 111 differs: A = B = 1 activates (good p = 0), C = 1 propagates. That one vector is the test.

fault-reconvergent.title: A stem fault whose effects reconverge and cancel
fault-reconvergent.intro: f = AB + A′C as g1 = AND(A, B), g2 = AND(A′, C), f = OR(g1, g2). Line A is stuck at 0. Each line shows good/faulty values.

elements.text: A stem fault on two reconvergent paths (A s-a-0)

steps.caption: f = AB + A′C. The stem A feeds g1 directly and g2 through an inverter. The fault: the stem A stuck-at-0, so both branches see 0.
The obvious test, A B C = 1 1 1: activate A (good 1) and open g1 (B = 1). But C = 1 also opens g2 to the faulty A′ = 1.
g1 = 1/0 and g2 = 0/1: the error and its complement reach the OR together, so f = 1/1. The two paths cancel; 111 is not a test.
A B C = 1 1 0: only one path is open, through g1 (C = 0 closes g2). f = 1/0: the outputs differ, a test.
A B C = 1 0 1: only one path is open, through g2 (B = 0 closes g1). f = 0/1: the outputs differ, a test.
∂f/∂A = B ⊕ C, so the stem tests are A = 1, B ≠ C: 101 and 110 only. The branch into g1 alone has tests 110 and 111.

five-var-map.title: A five-variable K-map as two four-variable maps
five-var-map.intro: f(A, B, C, D, E) = Σm(0, 2, 7, 8, 10, 11, 14, 15, 16, 18, 24, 26, 27, 30, 31), drawn as an A = 0 map and an A = 1 map (rows B C, columns D E).

elements.text: Five variables: two 4-variable maps, A = 0 and A = 1

steps.caption: A 5-variable map is two 4-variable maps (rows B C, columns D E), one for A = 0 and one for A = 1. Inside each map the usual neighbours apply; in addition every cell is adjacent to the cell in the same position of the other map (they differ only in A).

set.text: same position in the other map = neighbour

steps.caption: The four corner cells of each map (C = 0, E = 0) are 1s in both maps. In each map they form a corner quad, and the two quads face each other: one group of 8 = 2³ cells, so 5 − 3 = 2 literals: C′E′.
Rows B C = 11 and 10, columns D E = 11 and 10 (B = 1, D = 1) are 1s in both maps: another octet across the maps, BD.
Remaining: m7 (00111) in the A = 0 map only. Its twin m23 is 0, so the loop cannot cross to A = 1; inside its own map it pairs with m15: A′CDE (4 literals).

set.text: twin cell is 0: the pair stays in one map

fixed-point-bits.title: Bit weights in a 5.3 fixed-point byte
fixed-point-bits.intro: Eight bit cells b7 to b0 with the binary point between b3 and b2. Weights above the point are 16, 8, 4, 2, 1; below it ½, ¼, ⅛. The pattern 01011.010 is 8 + 2 + 1 + ¼ = 11.25. The format covers 0 to 31.875 in steps of ⅛.

elements.text: Unsigned 5.3 fixed point: b₇ … b₃ . b₂ b₁ b₀
range 0 … 31.875 in steps of ⅛ (2⁸ = 256 values)

fixed-point-ruler.title: Fixed point: the range–resolution trade-off
fixed-point-ruler.intro: A number line from 0 to 16 with sixteen tick marks, one for each 4-bit pattern. Each step moves the binary point one place left.

elements.text: 4 bits, point moved: range shrinks, steps get finer

steps.caption: With 0 fraction bits (4.0 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 1 from 0 to 15: resolution 1, largest value 15 = 2⁴ − 1.
With 1 fraction bit (3.1 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.5 from 0 to 7.5: resolution 0.5, largest value 7.5 = 2³ − 0.5.
With 2 fraction bits (2.2 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.25 from 0 to 3.75: resolution 0.25, largest value 3.75 = 2² − 0.25.
With 3 fraction bits (1.3 format) the 16 patterns are the multiples of 0.125 from 0 to 1.875: resolution 0.125, largest value 1.875 = 2¹ − 0.125.
The count of values never changes: n bits always give 2ⁿ = 16 patterns. Moving the point only trades range for resolution.

fp-align-add.title: Floating-point addition: align, add, normalise, round
fp-align-add.intro: Two numbers in a toy format with 4 fraction bits: A = 7 = 1.1100 × 2² and B = 1.625 = 1.1010 × 2⁰.

steps.caption: Write both significands with their hidden 1 and two extra guard positions. A = 1.1100 × 2², B = 1.1010 × 2⁰. The exponents differ by 2.
Align: shift the smaller number right by 2 and raise its exponent to 2. B becomes 0.0110 × 2², and the bits shifted out (1 0) land in the guard and round positions instead of being lost.
Add the aligned significands: 1.1100 00 + 0.0110 10 = 10.0010 10. The sum overflowed into a second integer bit.
Normalise: 10.0010 10 has two bits before the point, so shift right by 1 and add 1 to the exponent: 1.0001 010 × 2³. The bit shifted out joins the extra bits: G = 0, R = 1.
Round to nearest even: the guard bit is 0, so the extra bits are less than half an ulp and are dropped. Result 1.0001 × 2³ = 8.5.

set.text: stored 8.5; exact sum 8.625 (error 0.125, under half an ulp = 0.25)

full-adder-from-has.title: A full adder built from two half adders and an OR gate
full-adder-from-has.intro: Inputs A, B and Cin. HA1 adds A and B; HA2 adds HA1's sum and Cin; an OR gate combines the two half-adder carries into Cout.

elements.text: A full adder from two half adders and an OR gate

steps.caption: HA1 adds A and B: its XOR gives the partial sum p = A ⊕ B, its AND gives g = A·B (a carry made here).
HA2 adds p and Cin: S = p ⊕ Cin is the full sum, t = p·Cin is a carry made by passing Cin along.
The OR merges the two possible carries: Cout = g + t = A·B + Cin·(A ⊕ B).
A, B, Cin = 1, 1, 1: p = 0, g = 1, t = 0; S = 1, Cout = 1 (1 + 1 + 1 = 3); both carries can never be 1 together.
A, B, Cin = 1, 0, 1: p = 1, g = 0, t = 1; S = 0, Cout = 1 (1 + 0 + 1 = 2); both carries can never be 1 together.
A, B, Cin = 0, 1, 0: p = 1, g = 0, t = 0; S = 1, Cout = 0 (0 + 1 + 0 = 1); no carry is made.
A, B, Cin = 1, 1, 0: p = 0, g = 1, t = 0; S = 0, Cout = 1 (1 + 1 + 0 = 2); both carries can never be 1 together.

function-count.title: Counting Boolean functions: one free output bit per row
function-count.intro: A Boolean function is completely described by its output column. Count the columns.

elements.text: How many Boolean functions of n variables?

steps.caption: One variable: 2 rows. Each row's output is an independent choice of 0 or 1, so there are 2 × 2 = 2² = 4 functions: 0, x, x′ and 1.

set.text: a function = one output bit per row

steps.caption: Two variables: 4 rows, so 2⁴ = 16 functions, the sixteen of Lesson 1.
Three variables: 8 rows, so 2⁸ = 256 functions. In general n variables give 2ⁿ rows and 2^(2ⁿ) functions; for n = 4 that is 65 536.

gate-symbols.title: The seven logic gates with their truth tables filling row by row
gate-symbols.intro: NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, XOR and XNOR, each fed by the inputs A and B (NOT reads only A). The strip under each gate will hold its output for rows 00, 01, 10 and 11.

elements.text: The seven gates, row by row
The seven gates, row by row

steps.caption: Row 0: A = 0, B = 0. Outputs: NOT 1, AND 0, OR 0, NAND 1, NOR 1, XOR 0, XNOR 1.
Row 1: A = 0, B = 1. Outputs: NOT 1, AND 0, OR 1, NAND 1, NOR 0, XOR 1, XNOR 0.
Row 2: A = 1, B = 0. Outputs: NOT 0, AND 0, OR 1, NAND 1, NOR 0, XOR 1, XNOR 0.
Row 3: A = 1, B = 1. Outputs: NOT 0, AND 1, OR 1, NAND 0, NOR 0, XOR 0, XNOR 1.
Each gate's four outputs, read top to bottom, are its truth table: NOT 1100 (it reads only A), AND 0001, OR 0111, NAND 1110, NOR 1000, XOR 0110, XNOR 1001.

glitch-timing.title: Timing diagram of the X·X′ glitch
glitch-timing.intro: A signal X feeds an AND gate directly and through an inverter with a delay of 1 time unit. The AND gate is ideal (no delay).

elements.text: A glitch from a slow inverter: Y = X·X′

steps.caption: X rises at t = 2 and falls at t = 6. Logically Y = X·X′ is always 0.
The inverter takes one time unit, so X′ falls only at t = 3 and rises only at t = 7.
Between t = 2 and t = 3 both AND inputs are 1, so Y pulses to 1 for exactly the inverter delay: a static-0 hazard (a glitch).

set.text: 1-pulse of width = inverter delay on the rising edge

steps.caption: On the falling edge (t = 6 to 7) X is already 0 while X′ is still 0, so the AND sees 0, 0 and Y stays 0. The glitch appears only after X rises.

set.text: no glitch on the falling edge

gradual-underflow.title: Gradual underflow: denormals fill the hole around zero
gradual-underflow.intro: The values from 0 to 1 of a toy IEEE-style format with a 3-bit exponent (bias 3) and 2 fraction bits. At first only the normal numbers are drawn.

elements.text: A toy float (3-bit exponent, 2 fraction bits) between 0 and 1

steps.caption: With normal numbers only, the smallest positive value is 1/4 (1.00 × 2⁻²) and the next one down is 0. Just above 1/4 the values are 1/16 apart, but below it there is a hole four times wider.
Take x = 5/16 and y = 4/16, two different normal numbers. Their difference 1/16 falls in the hole, so a flush-to-zero machine returns x − y = 0 even though x ≠ y.
Denormals use the exponent field 0 with no hidden 1: 0.f × 2⁻², giving 1/16, 2/16 and 3/16. They fill the hole with the same 1/16 spacing as the first normal binade.

set.label: with denormals: evenly spaced down to 0

steps.caption: Now x − y = 1/16 is the denormal 0.01 × 2⁻², stored exactly. With denormals, x ≠ y always gives x − y ≠ 0.
The largest denormal, 3/16, is exactly one step below the smallest normal, 1/4. In IEEE single precision the same picture holds with 2⁻¹⁴⁹ steps up to 2⁻¹²⁶.

gray-converter.title: Binary to Gray and Gray to binary converters
gray-converter.intro: First: a binary → Gray converter (three independent XORs). Second: a Gray → binary converter (a ripple of XORs). The input is 1011.

elements.text: Binary → Gray and back, bit by bit (input 1011)

steps.caption: The binary input b3 b2 b1 b0 = 1011 enters. Each Gray bit XORs two neighbouring binary bits; the three XORs work at once.
g3 = b3 = 1: the MSB is copied unchanged.
g2 = b3 ⊕ b2 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1: the bits differ, so the Gray bit is 1.
g1 = b2 ⊕ b1 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1: the bits differ, so the Gray bit is 1.
g0 = b1 ⊕ b0 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0: the bits are equal, so the Gray bit is 0.
The Gray code of 1011 is 1110. To convert back, the Gray bits g3 g2 g1 g0 = 1110 enter the second circuit.
b3 = g3 = 1: the MSB is copied again.
b2 = b3 ⊕ g2 = 1 ⊕ 1 = 0: each binary bit needs the binary bit just found, so the decode ripples from the MSB down.
b1 = b2 ⊕ g1 = 0 ⊕ 1 = 1: each binary bit needs the binary bit just found, so the decode ripples from the MSB down.
b0 = b1 ⊕ g0 = 1 ⊕ 0 = 1: each binary bit needs the binary bit just found, so the decode ripples from the MSB down.
The ripple returns 1011, the original input. Binary → Gray needs no chain (each XOR is independent); Gray → binary is a chain of 3 XORs.

gray-reflect.title: Reflected Gray code, built by mirroring
